pages.x: The Boers, Dutch-speaking farmers whose families had trekked inland to escape British rule, had two republics, the Transvaal and the Orange Free State. In 1886 the richest gold field on earth was found in the Transvaal, and the city of Johannesburg sprang up. Thousands of foreign miners poured in, and Britain wanted control.

Paul Kruger, the Transvaal's stern old president, who had gone on the Great Trek as a boy, refused to give the foreign miners the vote, fearing they would swamp his people. After a failed British-backed raid in 1895 and years of pressure, he struck first in October 1899, and the Boers invaded the British colonies.

The Boers were tough horsemen and fine shots with modern German rifles. In one week of December 1899 they beat three British armies, and they besieged the towns of Ladysmith, Kimberley and Mafeking. At Mafeking Colonel Robert Baden-Powell held out for 217 days, and later founded the Scouts.

A young war reporter, Winston Churchill, was captured when the Boers ambushed an armoured train in Natal. He climbed over the wall of his prison in Pretoria, hid down a coal mine, and escaped to Portuguese East Africa on a goods train, buried among bales of wool. He came home famous.

A young Indian lawyer in Natal, Mohandas Gandhi, believing that Indians should show they were loyal citizens of the empire, organised more than a thousand Indians as stretcher-bearers. They carried wounded British soldiers from the battlefields, sometimes under fire.

Britain sent nearly half a million soldiers from across its empire and took the Boer capitals in 1900. But the Boers fought on as guerrillas, in small bands on horseback. To starve them out, the British commander, Lord Kitchener, burned some 30,000 farms and herded the women, children and Black farm workers into camps.

In the concentration camps, crowded tents with bad food and dirty water, disease swept through. Over 26,000 Boer women and children died, and many thousands of the Black Africans held in separate camps. A British woman, Emily Hobhouse, exposed the conditions and shamed the government into changes.
pages.of: Boer women and children died in camps

pages.x: The Boers finally gave in in May 1902. Their republics became British colonies, but were soon given back self-rule, and in 1910 they joined the Cape and Natal in the Union of South Africa. The peace left the Black majority, who had served and suffered on both sides, without any say.

It was Britain's biggest and costliest war since Napoleon, and it shook its faith in its empire. For Afrikaners the camps left a bitterness that fed their nationalism, and the white rule they built in the new South Africa led in time to apartheid.
